title: Ancient DNA From 521 Woolly Mammoths Reveals Ice Age Humans Hunted Females, Plus a First-Ever Chromosomal Anomaly
excerpt: The largest ancient DNA study of woolly mammoths shows Ice Age humans targeted female-led herds, while one specimen from Wrangel Island carried a sex chromosome combination never before documented in an extinct species.
body:
• Ancient DNA from 521 woolly mammoths — 448 newly sequenced — shows Ice Age humans disproportionately hunted females, likely by tracking predictable herd migration routes.
  • At natural death sites, 66 percent of mammoth remains were male; at human butchering sites from 30,000 to 20,000 years ago, 70 percent were female.
  • One mammoth from Wrangel Island carried X0/XX mosaicism, equivalent to Turner syndrome in humans — the first time such a chromosomal condition has been identified in an extinct species.
  • The study, published in Current Biology, was made possible by recent advances in ancient DNA methods and improved reference genomes.

Ice Age humans selectively hunted female woolly mammoths, according to the largest ancient DNA analysis of the species ever conducted. The study also uncovered a mammoth with a sex chromosome combination never before documented in any extinct animal.

A team led by Dr. Hannah Moots, a postdoctoral researcher at the Centre for Palaeogenetics in Stockholm, sequenced the DNA of 521 woolly mammoths from across Eurasia and North America. Of those, 448 were sequenced for the first time, making this the most comprehensive genomic survey of the species to date.

Female Herds Were Easier Targets

The sex ratios told a striking story. Among 421 mammoths found as isolated remains in natural settings — animals that appeared to have died without human intervention — 66 percent were male and 34 percent were female. But at roughly 100 bone beds identified as mammoth butchering sites dating from 30,000 to 20,000 years ago, the pattern reversed: 70 percent of the remains were female and only 30 percent were male.

The researchers do not believe hunters targeted females simply because they were smaller. Instead, they point to the behaviour of modern elephants as an explanation.

"If mammoths travelled in herds like modern elephants, they may have moved across the landscape in more predictable or seasonal ways. Adult males tend to wander more, whereas female-led herds follow more regular movement patterns, which may have made them easier to locate."

— Dr. Hannah Moots, Centre for Palaeogenetics

How Ice Age humans managed to bring down animals standing up to 3.7 metres tall and weighing upwards of eight tonnes remains an open question. Dr. David Díez del Molino, co-senior author and researcher at the Centre for Palaeogenetics, noted that tracking migration patterns and corralling mammoths into dead ends seems the most plausible strategy — and would help explain the overrepresentation of females who likely travelled in larger, more predictable groups.

A Chromosomal First in Paleogenomics

Among the hundreds of specimens, one individual stood out. A mammoth from Wrangel Island — the remote Arctic outpost in northeastern Russia where the last woolly mammoths survived until roughly 4,000 years ago — was neither a typical XX female nor an XY male.

Instead, it carried a condition known as X0/XX mosaicism, in which some cells contain only a single X chromosome while others carry the standard two. In humans, this condition is called Turner syndrome. It marks the first time a sex chromosome anomaly of this kind has been documented in an extinct species.

"We certainly weren't expecting to find this, but it was really exciting."

— Dr. Hannah Moots, Centre for Palaeogenetics

Moots cautioned that the effects of the condition on the mammoth's appearance or fertility are impossible to determine from bone DNA alone. "In other mammals, the effects can vary considerably depending on the species and whether the individual is a complete X0 or an X0/XX mosaic," she explained. In horses, for instance, X0 individuals appear outwardly normal but are often infertile due to abnormalities in ovarian development.

Advancing Ancient DNA Technology

The discovery of the chromosomal anomaly was partly serendipitous, according to Díez del Molino, but it also reflects rapid progress in paleogenomics technology. Similar techniques were previously used to identify Turner syndrome and other chromosomal conditions in ancient human remains, most notably in a 2024 study by the Francis Crick Institute that found mosaic Turner syndrome in a 2,500-year-old British individual.

"This really wouldn't have been possible until the last couple of years," Moots said. "The combination of improved reference genomes and new ancient DNA methods is what made this discovery possible."

Implications for Modern Conservation

The findings carry weight beyond paleontology. The study adds to a growing body of evidence about the genetic decline of small, isolated populations — a pattern directly relevant to modern conservation. The Wrangel Island mammoths, in particular, have become a cautionary tale: previous research has shown the island's final mammoth population suffered a "genomic meltdown" driven by inbreeding and the accumulation of harmful mutations.

The study's insights into ancient human-animal interactions also resonate with ongoing debates about hunting sustainability and the role humans played in megafauna extinctions worldwide. Indian researchers have contributed significantly to ancient DNA studies in recent years, including work on South Asian megafauna and the genetic history of elephants — the mammoth's closest living relatives.

The team is now working with other researchers to integrate ancient DNA, isotopic data, and archaeological findings to better understand how Ice Age hunters actually brought down these massive animals. The study is published in the journal Current Biology.
